topic: Station rules: antennas, beacons, transmissions, repeaters, third parties, automatic control (G1B, G1E; 22 pool questions)

notes.front: What counts as a station antenna structure under 97.15?
notes.back: The antenna and whatever holds it up, such as a mast or tower.
notes.explanation: Tall structures can be a hazard to aviation, so height above a threshold triggers outside notification (see the fact card).
notes.example: A 60-ft tower with a beam antenna is a station antenna structure well under the 200-ft trigger.

notes.front: What is PRB-1?
notes.back: The FCC ruling that state and local antenna rules must reasonably accommodate amateur communications and be the minimum practicable.
notes.explanation: Local zoning could otherwise ban antennas outright; PRB-1 sets a federal floor of protection.
notes.example: A town cannot cap every amateur tower at 20 ft if that height cannot support effective HF communication.

notes.front: What is “good engineering and good amateur practice”?
notes.back: The FCC's standard for anything Part 97 does not spell out.
notes.explanation: Rules cannot cover every situation, so this catch-all standard fills the gaps.
notes.example: Choosing a clear frequency before calling CQ is good amateur practice even though no rule numbers it.

notes.front: What is a propagation beacon?
notes.back: A station that transmits so others can observe propagation and reception; any Technician or higher may run one.
notes.explanation: A beacon gives a known, steady signal that listeners use to judge whether a path is open.
notes.example: Hearing a beacon on 14.100 MHz tells you 20 m is open to that beacon's location right now.

notes.front: What is a one-way transmission?
notes.back: A transmission not part of an exchange between two stations; normally barred, except for specific permitted purposes.
notes.explanation: 97.113(b) bars one-way transmissions except as specifically provided; amateur radio is meant for two-way communication, so broadcasting-style one-way use needs an explicit exception.
notes.example: Sending Morse code practice to no particular station is a permitted one-way transmission.

notes.front: What is a procedural signal (prosign)?
notes.back: A short code such as a Q signal or CW prosign that streamlines operating; allowed if it does not hide the message's meaning.
notes.explanation: Operators need to know the limit: brevity is fine, but a prosign used to disguise content is not.
notes.example: Sending “AR” to mark the end of a formal CW message is a procedural signal.

notes.front: What is retransmission, as the rules use the term?
notes.back: Repeating a signal that did not originate at your own station; generally restricted unless a rule allows it.
notes.explanation: Unrestricted retransmission could turn amateur stations into unlicensed relays for other services.
notes.example: Occasionally relaying a US government weather forecast is a permitted retransmission.

notes.front: What is a third-party agreement?
notes.back: An arrangement the US has made with another country's administration allowing amateurs to carry messages for people who are not licensed amateurs.
notes.explanation: 97.115(a)(2) lets emergency or disaster relief traffic go to any country, and exempts a third party eligible to be a control operator; an agreement opens the door for other international third-party traffic.
notes.example: Passing a message from a non-amateur relative to a station in a country covered by such an agreement.

notes.front: What is an automatically controlled digital station?
notes.back: A station sending RTTY or data emissions with no control operator present at the control point at the time.
notes.explanation: Automatic control lets a station run unattended, but the rules limit where it may transmit because no operator is watching for problems.
notes.example: A packet station left running overnight, replying to other stations without anyone at the keyboard.

notes.front: What is an FCC monitoring station?
notes.back: An FCC facility that monitors the spectrum; a station within 1 mile of one must avoid causing it harmful interference.
notes.explanation: These facilities need a clean listening environment nearby to do their job, so a special protection rule applies close to them.
notes.example: A ham living a half-mile from one of these facilities has to take extra care not to interfere with it.

notes.front: What is spread spectrum (SS)?
notes.back: A bandwidth-expansion modulation technique that spreads a signal across a wide bandwidth; limited to 10 W PEP for amateur use.
notes.explanation: 97.313(j) caps SS transmitter power at 10 W PEP output.
notes.example: A digital mode that hops across many channels each second, rather than staying on one frequency.

notes.front: What is Wi-Fi, in the context of the amateur rules?
notes.back: The common unlicensed wireless-networking service; amateurs may not use any part of the 2.4 GHz band to talk to Wi-Fi stations.
notes.explanation: Wi-Fi devices operate under a different, license-free set of rules, so amateur privileges do not extend to talking with them.
notes.example: You may operate amateur digital modes in the 2.4 GHz amateur band, but not to communicate with a neighbour's Wi-Fi router.

notes.front: What antenna structure height triggers FAA notice and FCC registration?
notes.back: More than 200 feet (60.96 m) above ground level.
notes.explanation: 97.15(a) also separately covers certain antenna structures located near or at a public-use airport.

notes.front: What two conditions must a local antenna regulation meet under PRB-1?
notes.back: It must reasonably accommodate amateur communications, and be the minimum practicable to meet the local purpose.
notes.explanation: Both conditions must hold; a rule that meets only one still fails PRB-1.

notes.front: Who decides what counts as good engineering and good amateur practice?
notes.back: The FCC.
notes.explanation: The pool keys the FCC; 97.101(a) sets the standard but names no body as its judge.

notes.front: What is the FCC-recognised purpose of a beacon station?
notes.back: Observation of propagation and reception, or other related experimental activities.
notes.explanation: 97.3(a)(9) names observation of propagation and reception (and related experiments); repeater ID and bulletins are not beacon purposes.

notes.front: How many beacons may transmit at once from one station location on one band?
notes.back: Only one; a beacon must not concurrently transmit on more than one channel in the same band from the same location.
notes.explanation: This limits one location's footprint on any given band to a single beacon signal.

notes.front: What is the maximum transmitter power for a beacon?
notes.back: 100 W (the rule says power must not exceed 100 W).
notes.explanation: The pool phrases it as “100 watts PEP output”, but the rule text itself just says 100 W.

notes.front: Where may an automatically controlled beacon transmit on HF?
notes.back: Only 28.20–28.30 MHz; elsewhere it needs local or remote control.
notes.explanation: Above HF, several more automatic-beacon segments exist, but only this one on HF.

notes.front: Why should you normally avoid transmitting on 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz?
notes.back: A system of propagation beacon stations operates on those frequencies.
notes.explanation: Transmitting there could interfere with the beacon network other operators rely on for propagation checks.

notes.front: What retransmission is permitted for all amateur stations?
notes.back: Occasional retransmission of weather and propagation forecast information from US government stations.
notes.explanation: The rule allows only occasional use, not a regular automatic relay service.

notes.front: What one-way transmission helps people learn Morse code?
notes.back: Transmissions necessary to assist persons learning, or improving proficiency in, the international Morse code.
notes.explanation: This is one of the specific exceptions to the general ban on one-way transmissions.

notes.front: What is the rule on abbreviations and procedural signals?
notes.back: They may be used, provided they do not obscure the meaning of a message.
notes.explanation: The rule sets a purpose test, not a fixed list of allowed codes.

notes.front: With which foreign amateurs may a US station communicate?
notes.back: Any country except one whose administration has notified the ITU that it objects to such communications.
notes.explanation: The default is permission; the exception is a specific ITU objection, not a requirement for a treaty.

notes.front: What operator class must control a 10 m repeater retransmitting a Technician's 2 m signal?
notes.back: General class or higher.
notes.explanation: 97.205(a) subjects the control operator to the privileges of the class held; Technician 10 m privileges (97.301(e)) are only 28.0-28.5 MHz, not the whole band.

notes.front: What must be true to contact an automatically controlled digital station outside the automatic-control segments?
notes.back: The initiating station must be under local or remote control.
notes.explanation: The rule blocks two unattended automatic stations from starting a contact with each other outside those bands.

notes.front: On what bands may automatically controlled digital stations communicate with each other?
notes.back: 6 m and shorter wavelength bands, plus limited segments of some HF bands.
notes.explanation: The HF segments are narrow and specific; outside them, automatic-to-automatic contact is not allowed.

notes.front: What three conditions require specific steps to avoid harmful interference?
notes.back: Within 1 mile of an FCC monitoring station; on a secondary-allocation band; transmitting spread spectrum.
notes.explanation: Each condition raises the risk of interference to a protected user, so the rules add extra care in each case.

notes.front: What disqualifies a third party from participating in an amateur message?
notes.back: Having had an amateur licence revoked and not reinstated.
notes.explanation: The rule bars specific past compliance failures, not nationality or the language spoken.

notes.front: What may a third-party message under an agreement be about?
notes.back: Amateur radio, remarks of a personal character, or emergencies and disaster relief.
notes.explanation: This is broader than “emergencies only”, and sets no fixed time limit.

notes.front: When may third-party messages be sent via remote control?
notes.back: Under any circumstances in which third-party messages are otherwise permitted by FCC rules.
notes.explanation: Remote control does not add extra restriction on top of the ordinary third-party rules.

notes.front: Which ITU region covers radio amateurs in North and South America?
notes.back: Region 2.
notes.explanation: The ITU divides the world into three numbered radio regions; the pool tests only this one grouping directly.

notes.front: What part of the 2.4 GHz amateur band may be used to talk to unlicensed Wi-Fi stations?
notes.back: No part of it.
notes.explanation: The amateur allocation and the licence-free Wi-Fi service are separate; amateur privileges do not cover talking to Wi-Fi devices.

notes.front: What is the maximum PEP output for spread spectrum transmissions?
notes.back: 10 W PEP.
notes.explanation: This is far below the 1.5 kW limit that applies elsewhere (97.313(b),(j)).

notes.front: What is the maximum height above ground for an antenna structure not near a public use airport without requiring notification to the FAA and registration with the FCC?
notes.back: 200 feet
notes.choices:
A) 50 feet
B) 100 feet
C) 200 feet
D) 250 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A: too low; not the rule threshold. B: too low; not the rule threshold. D: too high; not the rule threshold.
notes.explanation: 97.15(a) sets the threshold at more than 200 ft (60.96 m).

notes.front: With which of the following conditions must beacon stations comply?
notes.back: No more than one beacon station may transmit in the same band from the same station location
notes.choices:
A) No more than one beacon station may transmit in the same band from the same station location
B) The frequency must be coordinated with the National Beacon Organization
C) The frequency must be posted on the internet or published in a national periodical
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: no “National Beacon Organization” exists in the rule. C: the rule sets no posting requirement. D: only A is required by the rule.
notes.explanation: The rule limits one beacon per band per location; there is no such coordinating body or posting requirement.

notes.front: Which of the following is a purpose of a beacon station as identified in the FCC rules?
notes.back: Observation of propagation and reception
notes.choices:
A) Observation of propagation and reception
B) Automatic identification of repeaters
C) Transmission of bulletins of general interest to amateur radio licensees
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is a repeater function, not a beacon purpose. C: bulletins are a separate one-way transmission, not the beacon's defined purpose. D: only A is the rule's stated purpose.
notes.explanation: 97.3(a)(9) names observation of propagation and reception (and related experiments); repeater ID and bulletins are not beacon purposes.

notes.front: Which of the following transmissions is permitted for all amateur stations?
notes.back: Occasional retransmission of weather and propagation forecast information from US government stations
notes.choices:
A) Unidentified transmissions of less than 10 seconds duration for test purposes only
B) Automatic retransmission of other amateur signals by any amateur station
C) Occasional retransmission of weather and propagation forecast information from US government stations
D) Encrypted messages, if not intended to facilitate a criminal act
notes.choicesExplained: A: stations must always identify; there is no unidentified-test exception. B: only auxiliary, repeater, or space stations may automatically retransmit other amateur signals. D: messages encoded to obscure meaning are barred regardless of intent.
notes.explanation: 97.113(c) allows only occasional retransmission of government weather and propagation forecasts.

notes.front: Which of the following one-way transmissions are permitted?
notes.back: Transmissions to assist with learning the International Morse code
notes.choices:
A) Unidentified test transmissions of less than 10 seconds in duration
B) Transmissions to assist with learning the International Morse code
C) Regular transmissions offering equipment for sale, if intended for amateur radio use
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: unidentified transmissions are not permitted. C: sales notices are allowed only occasionally, not on a regular basis. D: only B is a permitted one-way transmission here.
notes.explanation: 97.111(b)(5) permits transmissions that assist learning or improving Morse code proficiency.

notes.front: Under what conditions are state and local governments permitted to regulate amateur radio antenna structures?
notes.back: Amateur Service communications must be reasonably accommodated, and regulations must constitute the minimum practical to accommodate a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity
notes.choices:
A) Under no circumstances, FCC rules take priority
B) At any time and to any extent necessary to accomplish a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity, provided that proper filings are made with the FCC
C) Only when such structures exceed 50 feet in height and are clearly visible 1,000 feet from the structure
D) Amateur Service communications must be reasonably accommodated, and regulations must constitute the minimum practical to accommodate a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity
notes.choicesExplained: A: local governments retain some regulatory power under PRB-1. B: regulation must still be the minimum practicable, not unlimited. C: no such height/visibility test exists in the rule.
notes.explanation: This is the PRB-1 standard: reasonable accommodation plus minimum practicable regulation.

notes.front: What are the restrictions on the use of abbreviations or procedural signals in the amateur service?
notes.back: They may be used if they do not obscure the meaning of a message
notes.choices:
A) Only “Q” signals are permitted
B) They may be used if they do not obscure the meaning of a message
C) They are not permitted
D) They are limited to those expressly listed in Part 97 of the FCC rules
notes.choicesExplained: A: CW prosigns and other codes are allowed too, not just Q signals. C: they are permitted, subject to the meaning test. D: Part 97 lists no fixed set of allowed abbreviations.
notes.explanation: 97.113(a)(4) bars only using codes to obscure meaning, not procedural signals generally.

notes.front: When is it permissible to communicate with amateur stations in countries outside the areas administered by the Federal Communications Commission?
notes.back: When the contact is with amateurs in any country except those whose administrations have notified the ITU that they object to such communications
notes.choices:
A) Only when the foreign country has a formal third-party agreement filed with the FCC
B) When the contact is with amateurs in any country except those whose administrations have notified the ITU that they object to such communications
C) Only when the contact is with amateurs licensed by a country which is a member of the United Nations, or by a territory possessed by such a country
D) Only when the contact is with amateurs licensed by a country which is a member of the International Amateur Radio Union, or by a territory possessed by such a country
notes.choicesExplained: A: a third-party agreement governs third-party traffic, not ordinary contacts. C: UN membership is not the rule's test. D: IARU membership is not the rule's test.
notes.explanation: A third-party agreement is needed only to relay third-party traffic, not for an ordinary two-way contact.

notes.front: On what HF frequencies are automatically controlled beacons permitted?
notes.back: 28.20 MHz to 28.30 MHz
notes.choices:
A) On any frequency if power is less than 1 watt
B) On any frequency if transmissions are in Morse code
C) 21.08 MHz to 21.09 MHz
D) 28.20 MHz to 28.30 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: power level does not create an exception. B: the emission mode does not create an exception. C: this segment is not named in the rule.
notes.explanation: 97.203(d) names 28.20–28.30 MHz as the only HF automatic-beacon segment.

notes.front: What is the power limit for beacon stations?
notes.back: 100 watts PEP output
notes.choices:
A) 10 watts PEP output
B) 20 watts PEP output
C) 100 watts PEP output
D) 200 watts PEP output
notes.choicesExplained: A: too low; not the rule's limit. B: too low; not the rule's limit. D: too high; not the rule's limit.
notes.explanation: 97.203(c) caps beacon transmitter power at 100 W.

notes.front: Who or what determines “good engineering and good amateur practice,” as applied to the operation of an amateur station in all respects not covered by the Part 97 rules?
notes.back: The FCC
notes.choices:
A) The FCC
B) The control operator
C) The IEEE
D) The ITU
notes.choicesExplained: B: the control operator follows the standard but does not define it. C: the IEEE has no role in this rule. D: the ITU has no role in this rule.
notes.explanation: The pool keys the FCC; 97.101(a) sets the standard but names no body.

notes.front: Which of the following would disqualify a third party from participating in sending a message via an amateur station?
notes.back: The third party’s amateur license has been revoked and not reinstated
notes.choices:
A) The third party’s amateur license has been revoked and not reinstated
B) The third party is not a US citizen
C) The third party is speaking in a language other than English
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: citizenship is not a disqualifying factor. C: language is not a disqualifying factor. D: only A disqualifies a third party.
notes.explanation: 97.115(b)(2) disqualifies on licence-compliance history, not citizenship or language.

notes.front: When may a 10-meter repeater retransmit the 2-meter signal from a station that has a Technician class control operator?
notes.back: Only if the 10-meter repeater control operator holds at least a General class license
notes.choices:
A) Under no circumstances
B) Only if the station on 10-meters is operating under a Special Temporary Authorization allowing such retransmission
C) Only during an FCC-declared general state of communications emergency
D) Only if the 10-meter repeater control operator holds at least a General class license
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is allowed under the stated condition. B: no such special authorization is required. C: no emergency declaration is required.
notes.explanation: The repeater's own control operator must hold General class or higher to use 10 m privileges.

notes.front: What is required to conduct communications with a digital station operating under automatic control outside the automatic control band segments?
notes.back: The station initiating the contact must be under local or remote control
notes.choices:
A) The station initiating the contact must be under local or remote control
B) The interrogating transmission must be made by another automatically controlled station
C) No third-party traffic may be transmitted
D) The control operator of the interrogating station must hold an Amateur Extra class license
notes.choicesExplained: B: the initiating station must not itself be automatically controlled. C: third-party traffic is a separate rule, not the requirement here. D: no specific licence class is required by this rule.
notes.explanation: 97.221(c)(1) requires the initiating station to be under local or remote control outside those segments.

notes.front: Which of the following conditions require a licensed amateur radio operator to take specific steps to avoid harmful interference to other users or facilities?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) When operating within one mile of an FCC Monitoring Station
B) When using a band where the Amateur Service is secondary
C) When a station is transmitting spread spectrum emissions
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: All three situations, proximity to a monitoring station, secondary status, and spread spectrum, trigger extra care.
notes.explanation: All three situations, proximity to a monitoring station, secondary status, and spread spectrum, trigger extra care.

notes.front: What are the restrictions on messages sent to a third party in a country with which there is a Third-Party Agreement?
notes.back: They must relate to amateur radio, or remarks of a personal character, or messages relating to emergencies or disaster relief
notes.choices:
A) They must relate to emergencies or disaster relief
B) They must be for other licensed amateurs
C) They must relate to amateur radio, or remarks of a personal character, or messages relating to emergencies or disaster relief
D) The message must be limited to no longer than 1 minute in duration and the name of the third party must be recorded in the station log
notes.choicesExplained: A: the allowed subjects are broader than emergencies alone. B: third-party messages are for people who are not themselves amateurs. D: no such duration limit or logging requirement exists in the rule.
notes.explanation: 97.115(a)(2)/97.117 give this broader subject-matter list, with no time limit stated.

notes.front: The frequency allocations of which ITU region apply to radio amateurs operating in North and South America?
notes.back: Region 2
notes.choices:
A) Region 4
B) Region 3
C) Region 2
D) Region 1
notes.choicesExplained: A: Region 4 does not exist in the ITU numbering. B, D: the pool keys Region 2 for the Americas; Regions 1 and 3 cover other parts of the world.
notes.explanation: The ITU divides the world into three numbered radio regions; the pool tests only this one grouping directly.

notes.front: In what part of the 2.4 GHz band may an amateur station communicate with non-licensed Wi-Fi stations?
notes.back: No part
notes.choices:
A) Anywhere in the band
B) Channels 1 through 4
C) Channels 42 through 45
D) No part
notes.choicesExplained: A: no part of the band is authorised for this. B: no such channel exception exists. C: no such channel exception exists.
notes.explanation: Amateur privileges do not extend to communicating with a separate, unlicensed service.

notes.front: What is the maximum PEP output allowed for spread spectrum transmissions?
notes.back: 10 watts
notes.choices:
A) 100 milliwatts
B) 10 watts
C) 100 watts
D) 1500 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A: too low; not the rule's limit. C: too high; not the rule's limit. D: 1500 W is the overall maximum (97.313(b)), not the SS limit.
notes.explanation: 97.313(j) caps spread spectrum at 10 W PEP.

notes.front: Why should an amateur operator normally avoid transmitting on 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz?
notes.back: A system of propagation beacon stations operates on those frequencies
notes.choices:
A) A system of propagation beacon stations operates on those frequencies
B) A system of automatic digital stations operates on those frequencies
C) These frequencies are set aside for emergency operations
D) These frequencies are set aside for bulletins from the FCC
notes.choicesExplained: B: these are beacon frequencies, not a digital-station network. C: no emergency set-aside applies here. D: the FCC does not reserve these for its own bulletins.
notes.explanation: These are recognised propagation-beacon frequencies, not emergency or FCC-bulletin channels.

notes.front: On what bands may automatically controlled stations transmitting RTTY or data emissions communicate with other automatically controlled digital stations?
notes.back: Anywhere in the 6-meter or shorter wavelength bands, and in limited segments of some of the HF bands
notes.choices:
A) On any band segment where digital operation is permitted
B) Anywhere in the non-phone segments of the 10-meter or shorter wavelength bands
C) Only in the non-phone Extra Class segments of the bands
D) Anywhere in the 6-meter or shorter wavelength bands, and in limited segments of some of the HF bands
notes.choicesExplained: A: the privilege is narrower than “any” permitted digital segment. B: the rule's segments are narrower than all non-phone 10 m and shorter. C: Extra-only segments are not the rule's defined set.
notes.explanation: 97.221(b) names 6 m and shorter, plus specific narrow HF segments.

notes.front: When may third-party messages be transmitted via remote control?
notes.back: Under any circumstances in which third party messages are permitted by FCC rules
notes.choices:
A) Under any circumstances in which third party messages are permitted by FCC rules
B) Under no circumstances except for emergencies
C) Only when the message is intended for licensed radio amateurs
D) Only when the message is intended for third parties in areas where licensing is controlled by the FCC
notes.choicesExplained: B: third-party traffic is not limited to emergencies. C: third parties are typically not themselves licensed amateurs. D: no such geographic restriction exists in the rule.
notes.explanation: Remote control adds no extra restriction beyond the ordinary third-party rules.

notes.front: How does the 100 W beacon power limit compare to the spread spectrum and general HF limits?
notes.back: Beacons: 100 W (97.203(c)); spread spectrum: 10 W PEP; general HF elsewhere: 1500 W PEP.
notes.explanation: Each emission type or station function has its own ceiling; do not assume the general 1500 W limit applies everywhere.

notes.front: Which HF segment is for automatic beacons, and which is where a 10 m repeater is allowed to operate?
notes.back: 28.20–28.30 MHz is for automatic HF beacons; 10 m repeaters operate above 29.5 MHz.
notes.explanation: Both lie on the 10 m band but in different, non-overlapping segments serving different functions.

notes.front: How does permitted government-forecast retransmission differ from third-party traffic under an agreement?
notes.back: Forecast retransmission relays a government broadcast occasionally; third-party traffic carries a private individual's own message.
notes.explanation: One is repeating already-public information; the other is carrying a message on someone else's behalf.
